why: SNOBOL4 is a 1960s string-pattern language with a strange, beautiful model of matching and backtracking.

brief.what_it_is: SNOBOL4 (StriNg Oriented and symBOlic Language) is a programming language for text processing and pattern matching. The homepage is a historical resource index for the language, not a README for one tool, so it does not say which implementation this Homebrew formula installs. The formula's description and executable names (snobol4, snobol4-2.3.4, sdb, snopea) suggest a command-line SNOBOL4 interpreter with a debugger and a companion tool, and the page's CSNOBOL4 entry is the likeliest match, but that is my inference and the page does not confirm it. Input is a SNOBOL4 program; output is whatever the program prints or computes.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents SNOBOL4 as a language first designed and implemented at Bell Telephone Laboratories in the 1970s for text processing, pattern matching, and much more. The page is mainly a preservation effort, collecting many historic and modern implementations, manuals, and books.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage does not explain the internals of any implementation, so I have nothing reliable to report on the mechanism. SNOBOL4's pattern matching, with its backtracking, is only mentioned in the scout notes, not on the page.
brief.install_notes: Nothing in the fetched page covers installation, configuration, or first-run steps. The page does list several implementations (CSNOBOL4 by Phil Budne, Macro SPITBOL, Oregon SNOBOL5, Minnesota SNOBOL4 for DOS, and others), so the exact source for the Homebrew build would need checking in the formula or upstream repository.
brief.standout: The page is a long, curated archive of SNOBOL4 implementations spanning IBM System/360, PDP-10, VAX, and CDC 6600 machines, plus books, mailing lists, and humanities work. Its own history section, which includes In Memoriam notes for Ralph and Madge Griswold, gives the language an unusual archival character.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage shows a visitor counter 'since September 1998' and a SPITBOL mailing list note 'as of 9/2021', which suggests the page was last substantively updated around 2021 or later. I found no release date or commit information, and I did not fetch a repository.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a resource index, not a project README, so it does not describe the Homebrew package's features or current version. The brew description says 1960s, but the homepage says the language was designed at Bell Labs in the 1970s; I could not resolve this from the page. The 2.3.4 version suffix and the sdb and snopea executables are unverified. Many links on the page are FTP links the page itself calls passe. The 'Other' and historical sections point to many implementations of uncertain current availability.

entry.title: SNOBOL4
entry.tldr: A string-processing language from Bell Labs where patterns are first-class values and matching backtracks. Odd, old, and a good way to see another model of text handling.
entry.deeper_look:
SNOBOL4 (StriNg Oriented and symBOlic Language) is a language for text processing, pattern matching, and much more. Its homepage says it was first designed and implemented at Bell Telephone Laboratories in the 1970s. The Homebrew description says 1960s, and the page does not settle the difference. The language itself is older than most tools you use.

This formula installs `snobol4` along with `sdb` and `snopea`, which look like a debugger and a companion tool. The brief could not confirm which implementation it builds. The likeliest match is Phil Budne's CSNOBOL4, described on the homepage as a port of the original Bell Labs Macro SNOBOL4 for machines with a C89 compiler. Treat that as an inference, not a fact. You feed it a SNOBOL4 program, and it prints or computes whatever the program says.

The idea underneath is that matching is a core part of the language rather than a library bolted on. The scout's notes point to a model of pattern matching with backtracking. The homepage itself does not explain the mechanism, so read the manuals it links to for the details. If you have only met regular expressions as strings inside another language, this is a different way to think about the problem.

The homepage is also a preservation project. It collects implementations for IBM System/360, PDP-10, VAX and CDC 6600 machines, plus books, mailing lists, and In Memoriam notes for Ralph and Madge Griswold. It is a decent starting point for the language's history.

entry.whats_unique: Pattern matching is built into the language itself, and the homepage doubles as an archive of implementations from mainframes to modern C ports.
entry.caveats: The homepage is a resource index, not a README for this package, so the exact implementation, version, and the purpose of sdb and snopea are unverified, and many of its links are old FTP links.
